subtopic: Caste and class awareness, discrimination recognition and fair conduct
passage: The rain in Kochi turned the lane into a river, and Anand's bus was forty minutes late for Ammamma's birthday lunch. He arrived soaked, holding a box of banana chips wrapped in plastic. Mahima's uncle shook his hand, asked his surname the way elders do when they want to know caste, and went silent. Through the whole meal the uncle spoke to everyone except Anand. In the kitchen Mahima hissed to her mother, "I'll tell him exactly what I think." Her mother kept wiping a plate. "Today? With Ammamma's cake on the table?" Mahima breathed out. Back at the table she sat beside Anand, passed him the payasam first, and said to the room, "We've been together two years. We're serious." The uncle left early. Ammamma, though, asked Anand to come again next month and bring more chips.

qa.q: What did Anand bring to Ammamma's birthday lunch?
qa.a: He brought a box of banana chips wrapped in plastic.

qa.q: What was Mahima feeling in the kitchen, and what shows it?
qa.a: Mahima was angry and hurt on Anand's behalf; she hissed that she would tell her uncle exactly what she thought.

qa.q: Which choice worked better than the argument Mahima wanted, and why?
qa.a: Sitting beside Anand and calmly saying they were serious stood by him honestly without turning the birthday into a fight, leaving the family room to adjust over time.

qa.q: How might Ammamma see Anand by the end of the lunch?
qa.a: Ammamma seems warm toward him, inviting him back next month, which suggests not every elder shares the uncle's worry.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult in a cross-caste relationship facing a relative's cold anger and choosing patience, honesty and loyalty over winning the argument at once.

passage:
"Mumma, Tenzin's house has little flags on the roof. Blue, white, red, green, yellow!"
"Those are prayer flags, Charu."
"Why doesn't Tenzin have a puja shelf like ours?"
"Tenzin's family prays differently. They use beads and flags to say their prayers."
"Are their prayers the right ones?"
"Their prayers are right for them. Ours are right for us."
"Can I ask Tenzin to show me the beads?"
"Yes. Ask nicely, and then listen."
"Tomorrow! And I'll show my diya."

qa.q: What colours are the flags on Tenzin's roof?
qa.a: They are blue, white, red, green and yellow.

qa.q: What does Charu's excited "Tomorrow!" suggest Charu is feeling?
qa.a: Charu feels curious and eager, not afraid, and wants to learn about the beads and share the diya too.

qa.q: How did Mumma keep Charu's curiosity open?
qa.a: Mumma gave short, honest answers, said each family's prayers are right for them, and encouraged Charu to ask Tenzin kindly and listen.

qa.q: What might it be like for Tenzin when Charu asks about the beads?
qa.a: Tenzin might feel pleased and proud to be asked kindly, and get to share something from home with a friend.

grounding: It illustrates a young child noticing that a friend's family prays differently and getting simple, honest answers that keep curiosity open and free of fear.

"Pradeep, this plate goes to Rizwana Aunty, the blue door," Amma said.
"The one who sent sheer khurma at Eid?"
"The same."
Pradeep balanced the steel plate of laddoos. His cousin Darshan carried the second plate, for the Fernandes family.
"Why do we give them sweets? It's our festival," Darshan asked on the stairs.
"Because at Christmas Mrs. Fernandes gives us plum cake. And the khurma was so good."
Rizwana Aunty opened the door. "Arre, Pradeep! Happy Diwali, beta! Wait, wait." She came back with a small box of dates. "For your Amma."
On the way down Darshan said, "So the whole building has one big festival?"
Pradeep grinned. "Three big festivals. We just take turns cooking."

qa.q: What did Rizwana Aunty give Pradeep for his Amma?
qa.a: She gave him a small box of dates for his Amma.

qa.q: What was Pradeep feeling when he grinned about "three big festivals"?
qa.a: He felt happy and proud, enjoying the sense that the whole building shares its celebrations, not just his own home.

qa.q: What would you tell a child who wonders why sweets go to families of other faiths?
qa.a: Share them anyway, as Pradeep does: small, regular swaps of laddoos, khurma and cake build friendships that make later prejudice hard to believe.

qa.q: How might Rizwana Aunty have felt when Pradeep came to the blue door?
qa.a: She was clearly delighted, greeting him warmly and hurrying to send dates back, glad the sharing goes both ways.

grounding: It illustrates a child sharing Diwali sweets with neighbours who share Eid and Christmas food, and feeling part of something bigger than one home.

passage: Pranav, you asked if anyone ever teased me for being Hindu. Sit. I was fifteen, the only brown boy in my class in Leicester. One morning Gary held his nose when I opened my lunch and said my lot prayed to monkeys. The whole row laughed. I went hot, then silent. I wanted to disappear into my collar. Then Colin, a quiet boy who kept pigeons, said, "That's rubbish, Gary. You don't know a thing about it." At lunch Colin told Mr. Hughes, our teacher. That afternoon Mr. Hughes stopped the lesson and said plainly that what Gary had said was false and unkind, and asked if I'd like to tell the class about Diwali. I said no that day. The next year I said yes. Your Karthik Thatha still remembers Colin's pigeons, beta.

qa.q: Where was Karthik the only brown boy in his class?
qa.a: He was the only brown boy in his class in Leicester.

qa.q: What did young Karthik feel when the whole row laughed?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and silenced; he went hot, then quiet, and wanted to disappear into his collar.

qa.q: At the turning point in the story, why did Colin's choice matter?
qa.a: Colin spoke up in the moment and then told the teacher the same day, so Karthik was not alone and an adult could name the stereotype as false.

qa.q: How might Colin have seen what Gary did?
qa.a: Colin clearly saw it as ignorant and unfair, and though quiet, felt strongly enough to call it rubbish in front of everyone.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager mocked about his religion by classmates, and how a friend who spoke up and a teacher who named the stereotype as false protected him.

passage: Last March, after the fight near the procession, Yogesh stopped waiting for me at the gate. We had walked to school together since Class 3. His family goes to the temple at the end of our lane; mine goes to the church beside it. For a week he said "busy" and looked at his shoes. I was hurt, and part of me wanted to say something sharp about his people. I didn't. On Saturday I sent him a message: "Did I do something, or is it the stuff in town?" He called that night. His mother had been scared after the fight and had told him to keep his distance for a while. "I'm not scared of you," he said. "I know," I said. "Nobody in our lane threw anything." We walk together again now, a little quieter than before. I'm Sarika, and I learnt that asking beats guessing.

qa.q: Since which class had Sarika and Yogesh walked to school together?
qa.a: They had walked to school together since Class 3.

qa.q: What was Sarika feeling when Yogesh kept saying "busy"?
qa.a: Sarika felt hurt and confused, and was even tempted to say something sharp about Yogesh's community, but held back.

qa.q: What did Sarika's message get right?
qa.a: It asked honestly and left room for Yogesh to explain, instead of guessing or blaming him for what others did in town.

qa.q: Why might Yogesh have pulled away even though he was not scared of Sarika?
qa.a: His mother was frightened after the fight and told him to keep his distance, so he was caught between her worry and the friendship, which left him awkward and quiet.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager whose friend of another faith pulls away after local trouble and a family warning, and who keeps trust by asking honestly and not blaming the friend.

passage:
Note to myself, Sunday night. Vikas's mother.
Vikas has spent every weekend this month at Zubin's flat. Tonight, when he said he'd be at their Navroz dinner, I heard myself say, "Why always them? What will your Chacha say?" He went quiet and packed his bag anyway.
Honestly, I'm not sure what I'm afraid of. That people will talk. That he'll drift from our pujas.
After he left I phoned Zubin's mother to thank her for feeding him so often. She laughed and said Vikas always asks what their prayers mean and then tells them about ours.
What I did next: when he came home I didn't lecture. I asked what he likes about that family. "They argue about books, Ma, and nobody shouts." I told him I'd been scared of losing our traditions. He said he wasn't planning to lose anything. We're inviting Zubin for Diwali.

qa.q: Which dinner did Vikas say he would be at?
qa.a: He said he'd be at their Navroz dinner.

qa.q: What was Vikas's mother afraid of when she questioned the Navroz dinner?
qa.a: She was worried people would talk and anxious that Vikas would drift from the family's pujas, though she admits she isn't sure of her own fear.

qa.q: What went right when Vikas came home?
qa.a: Instead of banning the friendship or lecturing, she asked what he values in that family and admitted her fear, which opened a talk about values and led to a Diwali invitation.

qa.q: How might Vikas have felt when his mother said "Why always them?"
qa.a: Vikas was probably hurt and frustrated; he went quiet but still packed his bag, showing he would not give up the friendship.

grounding: It illustrates a parent worried about a child's close friendship across faiths who moves from a label to an honest talk about values.

subtype: Standing beside a neighbour under threat [Response]
passage:
Kamal's diary. Friday, 11 pm.
Someone chalked an ugly line on Devika Aunty's gate this evening, about her temple bell being "noise". Two boys on a bike shouted it again at eight. She is seventy and lives alone since Uncle died. I went over with Ammi's biryani as an excuse and stayed till ten.
We scrubbed the gate together. I called the police helpline, and the station sent a constable, who took a photo and noted the bike's colour. I also wrote in our lane group: "Devika Aunty has lived here forty years. If you see anything, call me or the police." Six neighbours replied. Farhan offered to walk her to the market.
I wanted to hunt those boys down. I didn't write that in the group. Anger at them won't keep her safe; people at her gate will.
She rang her bell at nine like always. I heard it from my room.

qa.q: What did the constable do after arriving?
qa.a: The constable took a photo and noted the bike's colour.

qa.q: What was Kamal feeling about the boys on the bike?
qa.a: Kamal felt angry enough to want to hunt them down, but chose to keep that anger out of the lane group.

qa.q: Why was Kamal's message to the lane group a wise step?
qa.a: It asked neighbours to watch out and to call the police, gathering company around Devika Aunty without stirring anger against anyone.

qa.q: What might it have meant to Devika Aunty to ring her bell at nine as usual?
qa.a: It suggests she felt steadier and less alone, safe enough to keep her own practice after neighbours stood by her.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who offers company, practical help and a calm public voice when an elderly neighbour of another faith faces hostility.

passage: In the town school at Hosur, Sudha raised her hand during the lesson on the moon. "Ma'am, is God real?" A few children gasped. Ayesha whispered, "Of course. Allah is real." Ramesh said his grandfather didn't believe in any god. Mrs. Nair put the chalk down. "People believe very differently, Sudha. Many people in this room believe in God, in different ways. Some people don't. It's a big question, and you can keep asking it." At home that evening Sudha asked Paati, who was lighting the lamp. Paati said, "God is real to me, kanna. When you're older you'll think about it yourself." Sudha lay on the mat, looking at the ceiling fan, turning both answers over like two smooth stones.

qa.q: Who was lighting the lamp when Sudha asked at home?
qa.a: Paati was lighting the lamp.

qa.q: What might Sudha be feeling as she lies on the mat turning both answers over?
qa.a: Sudha seems curious and thoughtful rather than scared, calmly comparing the two answers.

qa.q: How did Mrs. Nair's reply protect Sudha's curiosity?
qa.a: She answered calmly and honestly that people believe differently, did not scold the question, and said Sudha could keep asking.

qa.q: How might Ayesha have felt when the teacher said some people don't believe in God?
qa.a: Ayesha, sure that Allah is real, might have felt surprised or unsettled, but the calm answer also respected her own belief.

grounding: It illustrates a child asking whether God is real and getting different but calm, honest answers at school and at home that keep curiosity and trust safe.
